p: You may have seen a report telling you that your website fails Core Web Vitals, with three abbreviations and a lot of orange and red. For a business owner it can feel like a language you were never taught. The idea behind it, however, is simple: Google measures three things that describe how a page feels to a real visitor, and it publishes targets for each.

This article explains what the three metrics are in everyday language, what counts as a good result, where the numbers come from, and which fixes tend to help most. It goes deeper into the measurements than a general speed guide, so you can read a report and know what to ask your developer to change.

Core Web Vitals are a small set of metrics that describe the user experience of a page: how quickly the main content appears, how quickly the page responds when someone interacts with it, and how stable the layout is while it loads. They are part of what Google calls page experience, and they are measured from real visits by real people using browsers such as Chrome.

There are currently three: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), Interaction to Next Paint (INP) and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS). Each has a threshold for good, one for needs improvement and one for poor. A page passes when at least 75 percent of visits meet the good threshold for each metric, measured over a period of time. In other words, the standard is about most of your visitors on most of their devices, not about the best case on your office computer.

h: Largest Contentful Paint: how fast the main content appears
p: LCP measures how long it takes for the biggest visible element in the first screen to render. That is usually a hero image, a large heading or a block of text. It stands in for the moment when a visitor feels that the page has loaded. A good LCP is 2.5 seconds or less. Above 4 seconds is considered poor.
The most frequent causes of slow LCP are oversized or unoptimised images, slow server responses, render-blocking CSS and JavaScript, and web fonts that load late. Each has a clear remedy.
list: Compress and resize the main image, serve modern formats such as WebP or AVIF, and make sure the browser downloads a size close to what it displays.
Do not lazy-load the main image above the fold. Instead, tell the browser it is important, for example by preloading it or giving it a high fetch priority.
Reduce server response time with good hosting, caching and a content delivery network.
Keep critical CSS small and load non-essential scripts later.
Host fonts yourself where possible and avoid loading more font weights than you use.

h: Interaction to Next Paint: how quickly the page responds
p: INP replaced an older metric called First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital in 2024. Where the old metric looked only at the first interaction, INP looks at the responsiveness of all clicks, taps and key presses during a visit, and reports a value close to the slowest. A good INP is 200 milliseconds or less, and above 500 milliseconds is poor.

In plain terms, INP asks: when someone taps a button, how long before the page visibly reacts? Slow responses are usually caused by the browser being busy running JavaScript. Large frameworks, many third-party scripts such as chat widgets and trackers, and heavy work triggered on every click all keep the main thread occupied.
list: Remove scripts you do not need. Every third-party tag has a cost, so review them regularly.
Split large JavaScript bundles so that each page loads only what it uses.
Break long tasks into smaller pieces so the browser can respond between them.
Keep the work done during an interaction small, and show immediate feedback, such as a pressed state or a spinner, before slow work finishes.

h: Cumulative Layout Shift: how stable the page is
p: CLS measures unexpected movement of content while the page loads or changes. You have felt this when you were about to tap a button and the page jumped, so you hit an advert instead. A good CLS score is 0.1 or lower, and above 0.25 is poor. Unlike the other two, it is a unitless score rather than a time.

The main causes are images and videos without declared dimensions, adverts or embeds that load late and push content down, banners and cookie notices inserted above existing content, and web fonts that swap in with a different size.
list: Always set width and height, or an aspect ratio, on images, videos and embeds so the browser reserves space.
Reserve space for adverts and widgets, even before they load.
Place banners and notices in an overlay or in space that was already reserved, instead of pushing the page down.
Use font-display settings and size-matched fallback fonts to reduce shifts when fonts load.

p: A common source of confusion is that different tools show different numbers. This usually comes from the difference between field data and lab data. Field data is collected from real users and is what Google uses to assess your pages. It appears in the Core Web Vitals report in Google Search Console and, for pages with enough traffic, at the top of PageSpeed Insights.

Lab data comes from a simulated test run, such as Lighthouse. It is repeatable and ideal for diagnosing and testing fixes, but it uses an assumed device and connection, so it will not match your real audience exactly. Use field data to know whether you have a problem, and lab data to find and fix it. If your site has little traffic, field data may not be available yet, in which case lab results are your best guide.

h: A worked example: a small online shop
p: Imagine a small online shop whose product page has a large hero image of 2 MB, a chat widget, a review plugin and an email pop-up. Reports show a slow LCP, a poor INP on mobile and a layout shift when the review stars load.

A sensible plan starts with the biggest wins. Resize and compress the hero image and mark it as high priority to improve LCP. Remove the pop-up from the first few seconds and delay the chat widget until the visitor interacts, which frees the main thread and improves INP. Give the review block a reserved height so nothing jumps when it loads, which lowers CLS. After deploying, the team re-runs Lighthouse to confirm the change and watches the Search Console report over the next few weeks, because field data takes time to update.
This is an illustrative scenario, but the pattern of fixing the largest image, the busiest scripts and the unstable elements in that order applies to most small sites.

h: Do Core Web Vitals affect rankings?
p: Google has said that page experience, including Core Web Vitals, is one of many signals used in ranking. A rule of thumb is that great content that matches what people are searching for still matters far more than a perfect score. A fast but unhelpful page will not rank well, while a slow page with the best answer may still rank.

However, speed affects more than rankings. Slow pages lose visitors before they read anything, and unstable layouts cause mis-taps and frustration. Good Core Web Vitals are worth pursuing because they improve conversions and user satisfaction, with a possible ranking benefit as a bonus.

list: Optimising only the home page, while product, blog and booking pages that bring in traffic stay slow.
Chasing a perfect 100 in Lighthouse instead of fixing what real visitors experience.
Adding plugins and tracking tags without checking their cost, then wondering why INP got worse.
Lazy-loading the very image that should appear first.
Testing only on a fast office connection and a powerful laptop rather than a mid-range phone.
Open the Core Web Vitals report in Google Search Console and note which page groups fail and why.
Run PageSpeed Insights for your most important pages and read both the field and lab sections.
Fix LCP first: resize and compress the main image, preload it, and check server speed.
Audit third-party scripts and remove or delay the ones you do not need.
Set dimensions on all images, videos and embeds, and reserve space for dynamic content.
Test on a real mid-range phone over mobile data.
Re-test after changes and monitor field data for several weeks.

p: What replaced First Input Delay? Interaction to Next Paint (INP) replaced First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital in 2024. INP is stricter because it considers all interactions during a visit, not just the first.

How long until my fixes show up in Search Console? Field data is collected over a rolling period of roughly four weeks, so improvements appear gradually. Lab tools show results immediately, which is why they are useful for checking a fix straight away.

Do I need a developer to improve these scores? Some improvements, such as compressing images and removing unused plugins, can be done by a site owner. Fixes involving JavaScript, caching and server configuration usually need a developer.

My site has too little traffic for field data. What should I do? Use lab results from Lighthouse and PageSpeed Insights as your guide, and follow the same fixes. Field data will appear once your site receives enough visits.

list: Core Web Vitals measure loading (LCP), responsiveness (INP) and visual stability (CLS) from real visits.
Good targets are LCP at 2.5 seconds or less, INP at 200 milliseconds or less and CLS at 0.1 or less, at the 75th percentile.
Fix the main image first, then heavy scripts, then unstable layout elements.
Use field data to see whether there is a problem and lab data to diagnose and test fixes.
Helpful content still matters most for ranking, but a fast, stable page serves visitors better.
